claims.text: Cross-domain probe transfer can be framed as subspace selection over source-domain principal components rather than raw activations.
methods: Standardize source activations, run PCA, keep the top 100 PCs
Project activations onto a subset S of PCs, then train logistic regression (lambda=10)
Reference configurations: full-representation source probe, source probe on the top-100 PCs, target-trained probe on the top-100 PCs (5-fold CV)
results: The PC basis is computed only from source data, so selection over it can in principle happen before the deployment distribution is known
Subsets of PCs are orthogonal subspaces, which makes probes easy to train, compare and ablate
Selection rules can only reweight or discard directions already in the 100-PC basis
conditions: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual stream, activations mean-pooled over assistant tokens

claims.text: A target-guided greedy search over source PCs is a diagnostic upper bound on how well a source-trained probe can transfer.
methods: Forward greedy selection: add the PC that most improves target AUROC; probe weights are always fit on source data
5-fold CV over the target: select on non-held-out folds, evaluate on the held-out fold
Stop when no PC improves AUROC by more than 0.001
Control: top-k PCs by variance, with k matched to the greedy subset size
results: The greedy probe is an upper bound, not an unbiased OOD estimate, because selection uses target labels
The top-k control tests whether any advantage comes from size or variance rather than from which directions are chosen
conditions: Greedy search can miss jointly useful subsets
Its output depends on the stopping threshold

claims.text: Two weight-based rankings test hypotheses about which PCs transfer: those the source probe leans on, and those that discriminate the target.
methods: Standardized coefficient = |coef| x std of the PC
Source-PCA probe ranking (probe trained on source) vs target-PCA probe ranking (probe trained on target), both in the source-PCA basis
Train a source probe on the top-k PCs of each ranking; k comes from greedy run on the full target dataset
results: Each hypothesis predicts that its ranking should behave like the greedy reference
Target-discriminative transfer would imply acquiring a little target data is the remedy; source-discriminative transfer would imply regularization or compactness is the remedy
Table 2: the PCs with the highest source-probe weights are mostly low-index (PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12, PC4, ...)
conditions: The k-setting greedy run differs from the per-fold greedy subsets

claims.text: An interpretability-driven rule, in which an LLM judge scores PC descriptions for OOD deception usefulness, selects a subspace without any target data.
methods: For each of the top 100 PCs, show the 8 most and 8 least activating source examples to GPT-5-mini
The judge describes both poles and rates OOD usefulness from 1 to 10; scores of 5 or more are reserved for general strategies
Keep only PCs that got the highest observed score in both of two runs
Controls: full-representation baseline, matched-size top PCs by variance, and the complement of the selected PCs within the top 100
results: The judge sees only source examples, so its scores exist before any target data is collected
Agreement filtering trades recall for precision
Appendix E: most directions are described as lexical or stylistic and scored lower; fewer are described as tactics (for example defensive hedging), which are rated more general but noisy
conditions: Single judge model and single prompt
No causal validation of what PCs encode

claims.text: Restricting to the top 100 PCs is justified by interpretability, not by generalization.
methods: Measure alignment of each PC with SAE decoder features (andyrdt SAE for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct)
results: Alignment falls with PC index: Spearman rho = -0.857 for the best-matching feature and -0.917 for the mean of the top 10 features
The authors explicitly do not claim that low-index PCs generalize better
conditions: Measured for this model and SAE

claims.text: Preprocessing keeps all selection rules comparable in what they are allowed to see.
methods: Target activations are standardized with source mean and variance
Responses labeled ambiguous by GPT-4o are removed
results: Re-standardizing a target with its own statistics would leak target distribution information
Label counts (-1/0/1): Roleplaying 140/59/172; Insider Trading Report 218/194/61; Insider Trading Confirm 29/38/84; Sandbagging 379/375/246

claims.text: Deception is a good testbed because its targets vary in distance from the source, though some targets discriminate between rules better than others.
methods: Source: Roleplaying; targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging
results: Sandbagging is the most OOD target, differing in both topic and form of deception
Insider Trading Confirm is easy for the baseline, which limits how well it can discriminate between selection rules
Where the baseline already transfers well, there is little headroom
conditions: Conclusions from a single distant target should be treated with caution

items.question: Under what judge behavior would the two-run agreement filter of the interpretability-driven rule return no PCs at all?
items.answer: This happens if the set of PCs given the highest observed score in run one does not intersect the set given the highest observed score in run two. The rule keeps only PCs that received the top score in both runs, so disjoint top sets, for example because the runs' maximum scores or top-scoring PCs differ, leave an empty subspace.
rubric: States that the selection would be empty when the top-scored PCs differ between the two runs (no overlap)
Explains that the rule requires a PC to receive the highest score in both runs, i.e. an intersection

items.question: Why would the per-fold greedy reference be especially unreliable on Insider Trading Confirm compared with Sandbagging?
items.answer: After removing ambiguous labels, Confirm has only 38+84=122 examples, so each held-out fold has about 24 examples, while Sandbagging has 621 (about 124 per fold). Greedy selection on so few target examples makes AUROC gains noisy and prone to overfitting the selection. The baseline is also already strong on Confirm, so there is little headroom.
rubric: Identifies the small labeled sample (about 122 non-ambiguous examples, about 24 per fold) as making greedy AUROC selection and evaluation noisy or overfit
Contrasts this with Sandbagging's much larger count (about 621) OR notes the limited headroom because the baseline is already strong

items.question: If Sandbagging's deception signal lay mostly in directions with negligible Roleplaying variance, would even the greedy reference reach a high AUROC on it, and why?
items.answer: No. Every procedure, including the greedy search, can only choose among the top 100 PCs computed from Roleplaying. If the relevant directions are not captured by that basis, no subset contains them, so the upper bound itself would be low.
rubric: Says no, the greedy reference would also be limited or low
Explains that all selection is restricted to the top-100 source PCs, so directions absent from the source basis cannot be selected

items.question: How would noisy target AUROC estimates combined with the 0.001 stopping threshold distort the weight-ranking comparison in Section 4.3?
items.answer: With noisy AUROC, many PCs can appear to add more than 0.001, so the greedy search keeps adding PCs and inflates the subset size. Because that greedy size sets k for the source-PCA and target-PCA rankings, both rankings would then be evaluated with an inflated k, distorting the comparison.
rubric: States that greedy would add spurious PCs and inflate the subset size
Explains that this size is the k used for the weight-based rankings, so their comparison is affected

items.question: When would the complement control of the interpretability-driven rule be nearly uninformative?
items.answer: It is nearly uninformative when the interp-selected set is very small, for example only a couple of PCs. The complement then contains almost all 100 PCs and is close to the source probe on the top-100 PCs, so it says little about whether the removed directions specifically carry transferable signal.
rubric: Identifies the case where the selected set is very small
Explains that the complement then nearly equals the full top-100-PC source probe, so it adds little discrimination

items.question: If the judge never awarded any PC a score of 5 or higher, what would the interpretability-driven rule select, and why is that a problem?
items.answer: It would still select the PCs with the highest observed score, for example 4, because the rule is defined relative to the observed maximum. Under the prompt, scores of 1 to 4 mark directions the judge considers noisy, brittle or surface-level. The rule would therefore build a subspace from directions the judge itself rated unlikely to transfer.
rubric: States that the rule would still pick the top observed score (a low score), because selection is relative to the maximum
Notes that by the prompt's rubric such scores indicate noisy, brittle or surface-cue directions, so the selection would not reflect judged generality

items.question: The judge prompt describes the source setup as Roleplaying. Would the judge's OOD scores reliably flag directions specific to Sandbagging's form of deception, and why?
items.answer: Not reliably. The judge sees only Roleplaying examples and a Roleplaying setup description, and Sandbagging deceives through deliberately wrong answers rather than misleading statements. A direction relevant there may never appear among the source extremes, so it cannot be rated on that basis.
rubric: Says no or not reliably
Explains that the judge only sees source (Roleplaying) examples, while Sandbagging's deception takes a different form (wrong answers)

items.question: The source-PCA probe ranking is computed from source data alone. Why is the procedure as evaluated in Section 4.3 still not target-free?
items.answer: The number of PCs kept, k, is set by running the greedy method on the full labeled target dataset. The ranking is source-only, but the subset size uses target labels. That is why only the interpretability rule is presented as using no target data.
rubric: States that k is determined by greedy selection on target data
Concludes that the evaluated procedure therefore uses target labels, unlike the interp rule

items.question: Why does the sign of the Spearman correlations in Appendix C support using low-index PCs for the interpretability comparison?
items.answer: Both correlations are negative (-0.857 and -0.917), meaning SAE decoder alignment falls as PC index rises. Lower-index PCs therefore align better with interpretable SAE features, so they are more likely to be describable in natural language by the judge.
rubric: Notes that the negative rho means alignment decreases with increasing PC index
Links higher SAE alignment to better natural-language interpretability, which the judge-based rule needs

items.question: Why might the greedy subset for a target include PCs ranked low by the source-PCA probe's standardized coefficients?
items.answer: Greedy picks PCs by how much they improve target AUROC, while the source ranking reflects how much the source probe relies on each PC. A PC carrying transferable signal need not be heavily weighted on Roleplaying, and heavily weighted ones may be Roleplaying-specific.
rubric: States that the two procedures use different criteria (target AUROC vs source weight)
Explains that source-heavy PCs may be source-specific while target-useful PCs may have small source weight

items.question: Why is the interp-selected subspace likely to contain only a small number of PCs?
items.answer: The prompt reserves scores of 5 or more for general strategies and pushes most directions to 1 to 4. Appendix E reports that most PCs are described as lexical or stylistic and scored down. On top of that, a PC must get the single highest observed score in both runs, which shrinks the set further.
rubric: Cites the prompt or Appendix E: most directions get low scores and only a few (tactic-like) get high ones
Cites the requirement of the highest score in both runs as further shrinking the set

items.question: Why would one expect the target-trained 100-PC probe to score at least as high as the greedy probe on a target?
items.answer: Both are restricted to the same 100-PC basis, but the target-trained probe fits its weights on target data, while the greedy probe only chooses which PCs to use and keeps weights fit on source. The target probe can place weight wherever the target suggests, so it reflects the subspace's full target signal.
rubric: States that the target-trained probe should be at least as good (it indicates the ceiling of signal in the basis)
Explains that greedy keeps source-fit weights and only chooses PCs, whereas the target probe fits weights on target data in the same basis

items.question: Why is it not surprising that a top-k-by-variance control and the source-probe ranking would share many PCs?
items.answer: Top-k by variance picks the lowest-index PCs by construction, and Table 2 shows the source probe's highest-weighted PCs are mostly low-index (PC1 to PC12 dominate). The paper attributes that to low-index PCs carrying the most source variance. Both lists therefore concentrate in the same region.
rubric: Notes that both lists concentrate on low-index PCs (top-k by variance by definition; Table 2 empirically)
Gives the reason: low-index PCs capture most source variance, and the source probe is trained on that distribution

items.question: Would the interpretability-driven rule still use no target data if the judge were shown the 8 most and least activating examples from Sandbagging instead of Roleplaying?
items.answer: No. The judge's scores would then depend on target examples, so the rule would lose the property that its scores exist before any target data is collected.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that showing target examples makes the judge's scores depend on target data

items.question: Would the interpretability-driven rule still use no target data if the judge scoring were run three times instead of twice, keeping only PCs that got the top score in all runs?
items.answer: Yes. Extra runs still use only source examples, so the rule remains target-free; it would just favor precision even more over recall.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that the judge still sees only source examples (more runs only change the precision/recall tradeoff)

items.question: Would the source-PCA probe ranking become a fully target-free procedure if k were still set by the full-target greedy run?
items.answer: No. k would still come from greedy selection using target labels, so the subset size depends on target data.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that the greedy k uses labeled target data

items.question: Would the source-PCA probe ranking become a fully target-free procedure if k were instead set to the number of PCs the judge gave the top score in both runs?
items.answer: Yes. Both the ranking (source probe weights) and k (source-only judge scores) would then come from source data only.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that both the ranking and the judge-derived k use only source data

items.question: If target activations were standardized with source mean and variance, would the interpretability-driven rule remain strictly source-only?
items.answer: Yes. The transformation is fixed on the source, so no target distributional information enters the representation; this is the paper's setup.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that source statistics leak no target distribution information

items.question: If each target were re-standardized with its own mean and variance, would the interpretability-driven rule remain strictly source-only?
items.answer: No. Target-specific statistics leak distributional information about the target into the representation, blurring the line between source-only and target-informed procedures.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that target statistics leak target distribution information

items.question: Would the size of the top-k-by-variance control in Section 4.2 change if the greedy stopping threshold were raised from 0.001 to 0.01?
items.answer: Yes, likely. k is matched to the greedy subset size, and a stricter threshold would generally stop greedy earlier, giving a smaller k.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that k is matched to the greedy subset size, which depends on the stopping threshold

items.question: Would the size of the top-k-by-variance control in Section 4.2 change if the LLM judge's prompt were rewritten?
items.answer: No. In Section 4.2, k is matched only to the greedy subset size, which does not depend on the judge.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that the Section 4.2 control's k comes from greedy, not from judge scores

items.question: A team must deploy a deception probe on a new domain with no labeled target examples. Which of the paper's selection procedures can they actually run as specified?
items.answer: Only the interpretability-driven rule. Greedy selection needs labeled target data. The target-PCA ranking needs a probe trained on target data. The source-PCA ranking as specified takes k from target-guided greedy.
rubric: Chooses the interpretability-driven (judge) rule
Explains that greedy and target ranking need target labels, and that the source ranking's k depends on greedy

items.question: If the framework were reused with Insider Trading Report as the source, which part of the judge setup would have to be changed beyond recomputing PCA?
items.answer: The judge prompt's dataset description, which currently says the model is roleplaying in a simple scenario with a chance to lie, would need to describe the new source. The 8 most and least activating examples shown to the judge would also need to come from the new source.
rubric: Identifies the prompt's Roleplaying-specific setup description as needing rewriting
Notes that the examples and statistics must come from the new source (they are always source-derived)

items.question: Applying the method to a different model, what check should be redone before reusing the top-100-PC restriction, and why?
items.answer: The SAE decoder alignment versus PC index analysis should be redone for the new model, since the negative correlations were measured with an SAE for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The restriction is justified only if low-index PCs are again more interpretable.
rubric: Names the SAE decoder alignment vs PC index check
Explains that the restriction's justification (rho negative) was established only for this model and SAE

items.question: A researcher adds a new target on which the full-representation baseline already transfers nearly perfectly. Will this target help distinguish the interp rule from its controls?
items.answer: Little, if at all. As with Insider Trading Confirm, a strong baseline leaves little headroom for any selection rule to stand out. More distant targets are more revealing.
rubric: Says it will help little or not at all
Explains that a strong baseline leaves little headroom (as with Insider Trading Confirm)

items.question: If a new target dataset had the same label distribution as Insider Trading Report, roughly what fraction of its examples would the paper's protocol discard?
items.answer: About 46%. Insider Trading Report has 218 ambiguous responses out of 473, and the protocol removes all ambiguous responses.
rubric: Gives about 46% (218/473)
Explains that the protocol removes responses labeled ambiguous (-1)

items.question: A team with a small labeled target set runs the greedy procedure and reports its held-out AUROC as expected deployment performance. What should they be told?
items.answer: The figure is optimistic. Greedy subset choice is guided by labeled target examples, so it is a diagnostic upper bound rather than an unbiased OOD estimate.
rubric: States that the number overestimates (is an upper bound on) deployable performance
Explains that subset selection used target labels

items.question: If SAE alignment had increased with PC index (positive Spearman rho), which design choice would lose its stated justification?
items.answer: Restricting all selection to the top 100 PCs. That choice rests on low-index PCs being more amenable to natural-language interpretation.
rubric: Identifies the top-100-PC restriction
Explains that it was justified by low-index PCs being more interpretable (more SAE-aligned)

items.question: If greedy-selected PCs had transferred no better than the top-k-by-variance control of the same size, which conclusion would lose support?
items.answer: The conclusion that the identity of chosen directions matters, i.e. that a specifically transferable subspace exists. Any advantage would instead be attributable to subset size or variance.
rubric: Identifies the claim that a transferable subspace exists because of which PCs are chosen
Explains that the control isolates size or variance from direction identity

items.question: If the target-PCA probe ranking had behaved like the greedy reference, which part of the paper's motivation would be weakened?
items.answer: The motivation for the interpretability analysis would be weakened. That motivation is that transfer may depend on a property not captured by discriminability on either domain. Instead, the first hypothesis would hold and the remedy would be acquiring a small amount of target data.
rubric: Identifies the motivation for the interpretability analysis (a non-discriminability property)
Notes that hypothesis 1 would be supported, implying acquiring target data as the remedy

items.question: If the probe trained on the complement of the interp-selected PCs transferred as well as the interp-selected probe, what would be undermined?
items.answer: The claim that the interp selection isolates the transferable signal would be undermined, since the directions it discards would carry comparable signal.
rubric: States that the selected PCs would not specifically carry the transferable signal
Explains that the complement control tests whether removed directions carry transferable signal

items.question: If the matched-size top-PCs-by-variance probe matched the interp-selected probe, which alternative explanation could not be ruled out?
items.answer: That any low-dimensional projection of that size, or a preference for high-variance directions, explains the result rather than the judge's choices.
rubric: Names dimensionality reduction or high-variance preference as the surviving explanation
Notes that this means the judge's specific selection would not be shown to matter

items.question: If the source probe on all top-100 PCs had matched the greedy reference on every target, what would that imply about the value of subspace selection within the basis?
items.answer: Selecting subsets within the 100-PC basis would offer no headroom. Any benefit would come from the dimensionality reduction itself, which the top-100 configuration isolates.
rubric: States that selection within the basis would add nothing (no headroom)
Explains that the top-100 configuration isolates dimensionality reduction from selection

items.question: Does the paper show that the interp-selected probe outperforms the full-representation baseline on all three targets? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper describes the procedures and controls but reports no AUROC numbers comparing them, and it notes that Confirm has little headroom.
rubric: Answers not settled
Notes that no comparative AUROC results are reported (the paper is a framework description)

items.question: Does the Appendix C correlation (rho = -0.917) show that lower-index PCs are more relevant to deception? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The correlation measures alignment with SAE decoder features, i.e. interpretability, not deception relevance or transfer, and the authors disclaim any generalization claim.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that the correlation measures SAE alignment or interpretability, not deception relevance

items.question: Does the paper establish that the PCs the judge rates highly causally carry deception information used by the model? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The descriptions come from top-activating examples and judge verbalizations only, and no PCs were ablated during inference.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that the evidence is descriptive (examples plus judge) with no inference-time ablation

items.question: Does the paper support using the greedy probe's AUROC as an estimate of deployable OOD performance? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The paper frames it as an upper bound because subset selection uses labeled target examples.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Explains that selection uses target labels, making it an upper bound

items.question: Does the paper show that the source probe's highest-weighted PCs (Table 2) encode Roleplaying-specific features rather than the deception contrast? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Appendix D says whether those directions reflect the behavior or Roleplaying-specific features is exactly what the interpretability procedure is meant to address, and no result settling it is reported.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that the paper poses this as an open question for the interp procedure without reporting a result

items.question: Does Appendix E show that directions described as communicative tactics (e.g., defensive hedging) are reliable deception detectors? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The judge rates them as more plausibly general, but it also characterizes them as noisy and flags false positives from legitimate hedging, and no detection performance is reported.
rubric: Answers not settled
Cites the judge's own noise or false-positive caveats and the absence of measured performance

items.question: Does the paper show the subspace-selection framework works for deception probes on other model families? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. All experiments use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at layer 15 with one source dataset, and the authors leave other models as future work.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that only one model, one layer and one source dataset were studied

items.question: The judge prompt shows token activations for the extreme examples but never says which examples are honest or deceptive. Under what condition would a source probe trained on the interp-selected subspace fail even on Roleplaying itself, before any distribution shift?
items.answer: It would fail if the PCs that get the top OOD score do not separate honest from deceptive Roleplaying responses. The judge scores how general a direction looks, not whether it carries the source label, and the logistic regression is fit only on source labels. A subspace without source label signal leaves the probe nothing to learn, so it would sit near chance.
rubric: Says the probe could fail or sit near chance when the selected PCs carry little or no honest/deceptive separation in Roleplaying.
Explains that the judge never sees labels and rates only apparent generality, so a high score does not guarantee source discriminability, while the probe must be fit on source labels.

items.question: The judge sees per-token activations formatted as token<TAB>activation, while the probe uses activations mean-pooled over the assistant response. When would a judge's description of a PC be a poor guide to what the probe actually uses from that PC?
items.answer: It would be a poor guide when the PC's mean-pooled value is driven by diffuse, response-wide content rather than by the few strongly activating tokens the judge reads off. In that case the salient tokens behind the description, possibly diluted by averaging over a long response, are not what moves the pooled feature the probe weights.
rubric: Identifies the mismatch: the description rests on salient individual tokens, but the probe sees a response-level average.

Names the failure condition: the pooled value is dominated by many weakly activating tokens or broad content, or strong tokens are diluted by averaging, so the description does not reflect the pooled feature.

items.question: Appendix E says the judge lowers scores for denial-versus-admission directions that rely on markers like "Yes" and "No". On which target could this penalty discard genuinely useful directions, and why?
items.answer: Insider Trading Confirm. There the deceptive act is an explicit confirmation, when asked, that no insider information was used. A denial-versus-admission direction keyed to yes/no answers could therefore separate the classes on that target, and down-scoring it as a lexical cue would remove helpful signal.
rubric: Names Insider Trading Confirm.
Explains that Confirm's deception is an explicit denial or confirmation in answer to a question, so a yes/no or denial-versus-admission direction can track the label there despite being lexical.

items.question: Which target's reported results are most exposed to errors in GPT-4o's 'ambiguous' labels, judging by Table 1, and why?
items.answer: Insider Trading Report. GPT-4o's ambiguous filter removes 218 of its 473 responses (about 46%), a larger share than on any other dataset: roughly 38% for Roleplaying and Sandbagging and 19% for Confirm. Systematic labeling errors there would change the evaluated population the most.
rubric: Names Insider Trading Report.
Supports it with the removed share: about 46% (218/473), the highest, compared with about 38% for Roleplaying and Sandbagging and about 19% for Confirm.

items.question: The judge sees only the 8 most and 8 least activating source examples per PC. When would this exemplar choice mislead the judge about what a PC represents?
items.answer: It would mislead when a PC's extremes are dominated by a few idiosyncratic or outlier Roleplaying responses that do not reflect how the direction varies across the bulk of the data. The judge would then describe and score those quirks. The risk is real because the source set is small (a few hundred labeled responses), so 16 examples are a thin and extreme slice.
rubric: Says the judge is misled when the extreme examples are unrepresentative, for example outliers or quirks, of the PC's typical behavior.
Explains that only the 16 extremes from a small source set are shown, so the description reflects those cases rather than the direction as a whole.

items.question: Under the target-discriminative hypothesis, suppose the top PCs by target-PCA probe weight separate the target classes well but carry almost no honest/deceptive signal in Roleplaying. Would a probe trained on those PCs transfer well, and why?
items.answer: Probably not. In Section 4.3 the probe on the selected PCs is still fit on source data, so if those directions do not separate Roleplaying classes, the learned weights will be small or arbitrary. Target discriminability of a direction is not enough; the source fit must also align with it.
rubric: Concludes that transfer would likely be poor or unreliable.
Explains that the probe weights are fit on source labels, so directions without source signal get weak or arbitrary weights even if they discriminate the target.

items.question: Why does the orthogonality of PCs make the complement control in Section 4.5 cleanly interpretable?
items.answer: The selected PCs and their complement are disjoint sets of orthogonal directions that together span the 100-PC subspace. Projecting onto the complement removes exactly the selected directions and leaves the rest unchanged. Any difference between the two probes can therefore be attributed to which directions were kept, with no shared or leaked signal.
rubric: States that the selected and complement subspaces are orthogonal and non-overlapping, jointly spanning the top-100 space.
Explains that removing the selected PCs therefore removes exactly those directions without altering the others, so the comparison isolates the contribution of the selected directions.

items.question: Why is it unsurprising that Appendix E finds many PC descriptions framed in lexical terms, such as reliance on "Yes", "No" or hedging phrases?
items.answer: The evidence the judge receives is token-level: each line pairs a token with its activation on the PC. The most visible pattern is therefore which words light up, so descriptions naturally gravitate to lexical markers even when the prompt asks the judge to look past surface cues.
rubric: Points to the input format: the judge sees per-token activations, token<TAB>activation, for the extreme examples.
Concludes that the evidence highlights specific words, which pushes descriptions toward lexical patterns.

items.question: Why is the greedy probe an upper bound only relative to the top-100-PC basis, not relative to every linear probe that could be trained on source data?
items.answer: Greedy search only chooses among the top 100 source PCs. Any transferable signal in lower-variance directions beyond PC100, or in the full activation space outside that basis, is unavailable to it. The basis was chosen for interpretability, not because it covers all transferable directions.
rubric: States that the search is confined to the top 100 PCs, so directions outside the basis cannot be selected.
Notes that the restriction to 100 PCs is justified by interpretability rather than generalization, so useful signal may lie outside it.

items.question: The target-trained 100-PC probe uses target labels anyway. Why is it still built on target activations standardized with source statistics and projected onto the source PCA basis, rather than on a PCA of the target?
items.answer: Its purpose is to show how much target-relevant signal exists inside the exact subspace that source-only selection rules can use. Keeping the source standardization and source basis makes it directly comparable with those rules. A target-derived basis would measure signal in a different space that no source rule could ever access.
rubric: States that the probe measures target signal available within the same source-defined subspace the selection rules operate in.
Explains that a target-derived basis or standardization would break comparability, since source rules can only reweight or discard source-basis directions.

items.question: Why could PCs that top Table 2, such as PC7 or PC8, be absent from a target's greedy subset?
items.answer: A high standardized coefficient means the direction separates Roleplaying classes, not that its relation to deception holds in the target. If PC7 or PC8 encodes Roleplaying-specific correlates of deception, adding it would not raise target AUROC by more than 0.001. Greedy search would then skip it.
rubric: Explains that a high source-probe weight reflects source discriminability, possibly from scenario-specific correlates, which need not carry over to the target.
Links this to greedy selection: a PC is added only if it improves target AUROC (by more than 0.001), so source-heavy but non-transferring PCs are skipped.

items.question: Why do the weight-based rankings multiply each coefficient's absolute value by the PC's standard deviation instead of ranking by raw coefficients?
items.answer: PC projections have very different spreads, and variance falls with PC index. A raw coefficient on a low-variance PC can be large while barely moving the logit. Multiplying by the PC's standard deviation expresses each weight as its typical contribution to the probe's output, so PCs can be compared on a common scale.
rubric: Notes that different PCs have different variances, so raw coefficients are on different scales.
Explains that scaling by standard deviation reflects each PC's actual typical influence on the probe's prediction, making rankings comparable.

items.question: Is the per-fold greedy probe's held-out AUROC still an upper bound rather than an unbiased OOD estimate, given that the held-out fold itself is never used during selection?
items.answer: Yes. The PCs are still chosen using labels from the other folds of the same target distribution, so selection is fitted to that target. The held-out score therefore reflects target-informed selection, not what a source-only procedure would achieve.
rubric: Answers yes, it remains an upper bound or optimistic.
Explains that selection uses labels from other folds of the same target distribution, so the choice is still target-informed.

items.question: Would the greedy probe's target AUROC still be an upper bound rather than an unbiased OOD estimate if PCs were added based on AUROC on held-out Roleplaying data instead of target folds?
items.answer: No. Selection would then use only source data, making the procedure source-only. Its target AUROC would be an honest out-of-distribution estimate rather than a target-informed upper bound.
rubric: Answers no, it would no longer be a target-informed upper bound.
Explains that no target labels would influence selection, so the target evaluation becomes an unbiased OOD estimate.

items.question: Would the interp-selected PC subset be the same for Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm and Sandbagging?
items.answer: Yes. The judge scores PCs computed from Roleplaying using only Roleplaying examples, and the rule uses no target data. A single subset and a single source probe therefore apply to every target.
rubric: Answers yes, one shared subset.
Explains that selection depends only on source PCs and source exemplars, with no target data involved.

items.question: Would the greedy-selected PC subset be the same for Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm and Sandbagging?
items.answer: No, not in general. Each greedy step adds the PC that most improves AUROC on the particular target, and differs even across that target's CV folds. Different targets will generally yield different subsets.
rubric: Answers no, the subsets generally differ.
Explains that greedy selection is driven by each target's labeled AUROC, and per fold, so it is target-specific.

items.question: Would the top-100 PC basis change if the ambiguous Sandbagging responses were kept instead of removed?
items.answer: No. The PCA, and the standardization feeding it, is computed only from Roleplaying source activations. Target filtering affects evaluation, not the basis.
rubric: Answers no, the basis is unchanged.
Explains that PCA and standardization use only source (Roleplaying) data.

items.question: Would the top-100 PC basis change if the ambiguous Roleplaying responses were kept instead of removed?
items.answer: Yes. Those 140 responses would join the source activations used to compute the standardization statistics and the PCA. That changes the PCs and everything defined over them.
rubric: Answers yes, the basis would change.
Explains that Roleplaying is the source, so its retained examples determine the standardization statistics and the PCA (140 additional responses).

items.question: Does the matched-size top-PCs-by-variance control in Section 4.5 use any target information?
items.answer: No. Its size is set by the number of interp-selected PCs, which the judge determines from source examples alone, and its PCs are ranked by source variance.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that its size comes from the source-only interp selection and its ranking from source variance.

items.question: Does the top-k-by-variance control in Section 4.2 use any target information?
items.answer: Yes, indirectly. Its k is matched to the size of the greedy subset, and that size depends on target-guided selection over target AUROC. The PCs themselves are still ranked by source variance.
rubric: Answers yes, through k.
Explains that k equals the greedy subset size, which is determined using target labels.

items.question: On a new target, a team finds that the source-PCA probe ranking at the matched k behaves like the greedy reference, but the target-PCA probe ranking does not. Where should they invest effort to improve transfer?
items.answer: In regularization or a more compact source representation, not in collecting target labels. The result fits the hypothesis that greedy merely rediscovers the source signal in compact form, and the paper ties that hypothesis to regularization or compactness as the remedy.
rubric: Recommends regularization or compactness of the source representation, rather than acquiring target data.
Justifies it by the hypothesis that greedy recovers source-discriminative directions, which the paper links to that remedy.

items.question: Appendix E says many PCs are described as denial or deflection versus admission or detailed explanation. Should a team monitoring a Sandbagging-like deployment expect these directions to carry over well, and why?
items.answer: Probably not. Sandbagging deception consists of deliberately wrong answers rather than misleading statements about events, so there is typically no denial or admission to detect. Directions built around that contrast in Roleplaying are poorly matched to Sandbagging's form of deception.
rubric: Concludes that these directions are unlikely to transfer well to Sandbagging.
Explains that Sandbagging's deception is deliberately wrong answers, not denial or misleading statements, so the denial-versus-admission contrast does not fit.

items.question: A team using the interp rule finds that the selected subspace contains too few PCs to train a useful probe. Which step of the procedure could they relax to enlarge it, and at what cost?
items.answer: They could relax the two-run agreement filter, for example by using a single run or keeping PCs with the top score in either run, or accept scores just below the maximum. This raises recall but sacrifices the precision the filter provides, admitting more PCs that scored highly by chance.
rubric: Identifies relaxing the two-run agreement requirement, or the top-score-only cutoff, as the lever.
States the cost: more noisy or chance high-scored PCs are included (less precision, more recall).

items.question: A team has already built an interp-selected probe from Roleplaying and wants to apply it to a newly released deception dataset. Do they need to rerun the judge or recompute PCA, and what processing must the new data undergo?
items.answer: No, neither is needed. The subspace and the probe depend only on source data. The new activations just need to be standardized with the source mean and variance and projected onto the same selected source PCs before the existing probe is applied.
rubric: States that neither the judge nor PCA needs rerunning, because selection is source-only.
Specifies that new data must be standardized with source statistics, not its own, and projected onto the selected source PCs.

items.question: A team reuses the judge but deletes the prompt lines that call for low scores on surface cues and reserve scores of 5 or more for general strategies. How would the interp-selected subspace likely change?
items.answer: It would likely admit more lexical and stylistic directions. Appendix E shows these are numerous and are only held down by the prompt's instructions. The subspace would then be more likely to include directions that correlate with deception in Roleplaying through surface cues and transfer poorly.
rubric: Predicts that more lexical or stylistic PCs would receive top scores and be selected.
Explains that those instructions are what push such directions down (they are common per Appendix E), so removing them risks selecting non-transferable surface cues.

items.question: To cut cost, a team shows the judge only the 4 most and 4 least activating examples per PC instead of 8. What effect should they expect on the interp rule?
items.answer: Scores would likely become noisier and more driven by individual examples. The paper notes that the number of exemplars can change rankings, so fewer examples give the judge less evidence to separate general strategies from local quirks. More disagreement between runs would also shrink the set that survives the agreement filter.
rubric: Predicts noisier or less reliable descriptions and scores, possibly a different ranking.
Explains that less evidence per pole makes general and idiosyncratic patterns harder to tell apart, and/or that run disagreement shrinks the agreement-filtered set.

items.question: If the source probe on the top-100 PCs had transferred much worse than the full-representation baseline, which design choice would this call into question?
items.answer: The restriction to the top 100 PCs. It was justified only by interpretability, via SAE alignment, explicitly not by generalization. A large drop would mean every selection rule starts from a basis that has already lost transferable signal.
rubric: Names the top-100-PC restriction (dimensionality reduction to the PCA basis).
Explains that its justification was interpretability, not generalization, and that all selection rules can only use directions within that basis, so they would inherit the loss.

items.question: If the source-PCA probe ranking alone had matched the greedy reference on every target, what would that imply about the added value of the interpretability-driven rule?
items.answer: Its added value would be doubtful. Transfer would then be explained by source discriminability, with greedy just compacting the source signal. A simple weight-based ranking computed from source would suffice, needing only a way to choose k, and judging descriptions would add little.
rubric: Concludes that the interp rule's distinct contribution would be weakened.

Explains that transfer would then be captured by source-probe weights, which are source-derived, so the paper's motivation that transfer may depend on something beyond discriminability would lose force.

items.question: If the greedy probe had failed to beat the full-representation baseline on any target, what would happen to the case for searching for source-only selection rules within the 100-PC basis?
items.answer: It would be largely undercut. Greedy is a target-informed upper bound within the basis, so source-only rules over the same basis should not be expected to beat the baseline either. Greedy's possible misses on jointly useful subsets leave a small caveat.
rubric: Concludes that the motivation or prospects for source-only selection within the basis would be undermined.
Explains that greedy serves as an upper bound on what selection within the basis can achieve (allowing for greedy's limitations), so a weaker upper bound leaves no headroom.

items.question: If the target-trained probe on the top-100 source PCs were near chance on Sandbagging, what would follow for every source-trained selection rule on that target?
items.answer: None of them could be expected to do well there. Even with free placement of weights using target labels, the subspace would contain little Sandbagging-relevant signal, and selection rules can only reweight or discard those same directions. Poor Sandbagging results would then reflect basis coverage, not the quality of the selection rule.
rubric: Concludes that all source-trained rules within the basis would also be expected to fail on Sandbagging.
Explains that the target-trained probe measures available signal in the subspace, and rules can only reweight or discard its directions, so failures would reflect basis coverage.

items.question: If Appendix E had shown that the PCs with the top OOD scores were mostly described as relying on lexical markers or stylistic habits, which aspect of the method's design would be undermined?
items.answer: The claim that the judge prompt successfully pushes against overrating surface cues. The prompt is designed to give such directions low scores and reserve high scores for general strategies. The interp rule's premise of selecting behaviorally general directions would then fail.
rubric: Identifies the judge prompt's guard against overrating surface cues, and hence the interp rule's premise.
Explains that the prompt instructs low scores for surface or lexical cues, so top scores going to them would show the safeguard not working.

items.question: If the greedy subsets selected in different CV folds of the same target had overlapped very little, which design decision in Section 4.3 would this support?
items.answer: Running greedy once on the full target dataset to set k. Unstable per-fold subsets would give no single reliable size or PC set, and the paper chose the full-data run precisely to get one stable PC set.
rubric: Names the decision to set k from a full-target greedy run rather than per-fold subsets.
Explains that low overlap means the per-fold results are unstable, and the full-data run provides a single stable set.

items.question: If the interp-selected PCs turned out to be nearly the highest-variance PCs themselves (for example PC1 to PC5), which comparison in Section 4.5 could no longer separate explanations?
items.answer: The comparison with the matched-size top-PCs-by-variance control. The two subspaces would nearly coincide, so a difference from the baseline could not be credited to the judge's choices rather than to a preference for high-variance directions.
rubric: Names the matched-size top-PCs-by-variance control.
Explains that the two subspaces would be nearly identical, so the variance-preference explanation could not be ruled out.

items.question: Does the paper show that the greedy probe achieves the best target AUROC of any source-trained probe over subsets of the top 100 PCs? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted, as a guarantee. The paper acknowledges that forward greedy selection can miss subsets whose members are individually unhelpful but jointly useful, and that its output depends on the stopping threshold. It is therefore a practical reference, not the optimal subset.
rubric: Answers contradicted, or not guaranteed.
Cites that greedy can miss jointly useful subsets and depends on the 0.001 stopping threshold.

items.question: Does the paper show that its interpretability pipeline involves no design choice informed by cross-domain performance? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The judge step uses no target data, but layer 15 was taken from prior work because it had the highest cross-domain AUROC. The paper does not say which data that analysis used, so some target-informed choice upstream cannot be ruled out.
rubric: Answers not settled, or notes it is not strictly shown.
Points to the layer choice (layer 15), taken from prior work for highest cross-domain AUROC, as a possibly performance-informed upstream decision.

items.question: Citing Mu et al., the paper notes that removing top PCs can improve downstream performance. Does it show that the highest-variance source PCs carry spurious, non-transferring deception signal? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Mu et al. is cited as prior work, and the authors explicitly decline to claim anything about whether low-index PCs generalize better or worse. Table 2 shows only that the source probe relies on low-index PCs, not whether they transfer.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that the authors make no generalization claim about low-index PCs and that Table 2 reflects source reliance only, with no transfer test of those PCs reported.

items.question: Does the paper show that a transferable PC must be either strongly target-discriminative or strongly source-discriminative? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper tests these two hypotheses but explicitly raises a third possibility: transfer may depend on a property of directions not captured by discriminability on either domain. That possibility is what motivates the interpretability analysis.
rubric: Answers not settled, or not shown.
Notes that the paper explicitly allows a third possibility beyond discriminability on either domain, which motivates the interp rule.

items.question: Does the paper show that selecting subspaces in the source PCA basis transfers better than selecting SAE features? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. SAE decoder features are used only to measure how interpretable each PC is (the Appendix C alignment). No probe is trained on SAE features, so there is no comparison of transfer between the two bases.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that SAE features serve only as an interpretability check on PCs, and no SAE-based probe or transfer comparison is reported.

items.question: Does the paper show that PC1, the highest-variance direction, is the direction the source probe relies on most? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. In Table 2's standardized-coefficient ranking, PC7 comes first, followed by PC8, PC11 and PC12, while PC1 appears only 13th. High variance alone does not make a PC the source probe's most heavily weighted direction.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites Table 2: PC7 is ranked first, and PC1 appears far down the list (13th).

items.question: The target-PCA probe ranking orders PCs by absolute standardized coefficient, but the probe on the selected top-k PCs is then fit on source data. When could that probe score well below 0.5 AUROC on the target even though the selected PCs separate the target classes strongly?
items.answer: This happens when the selected PCs relate to deception with the opposite sign in the target as in Roleplaying. The ranking uses absolute coefficients, so it ignores sign. The weights are then fit on source data, so they point the wrong way for the target and invert the ranking of honest and deceptive examples.
rubric: Says the probe can fall below chance (inverted ranking) when the PC-label relationship has opposite sign in source vs target
Explains that the ranking uses absolute values (discards sign) while the weights, and hence the sign, are fit on source data

items.question: When would mean-pooling layer-15 activations over the assistant response make every PC-subspace selection rule miss deception on a target, no matter which PCs are chosen?
items.answer: This happens when the deceptive content sits in a few tokens of an otherwise ordinary response, such as a single wrong answer or a single false claim. Averaging over all assistant tokens dilutes that signal among non-deceptive tokens. Every rule selects directions in the same pooled vector, so choosing PCs cannot recover information that pooling has already washed out.
rubric: Identifies the condition: deception localized in a small fraction of the response's tokens
Explains that averaging dilutes the signal and that all selection rules act on the same pooled representation, so selection cannot restore it

items.question: Target activations are standardized with source mean and variance. When would this choice distort how target examples project onto the source PCs?
items.answer: It distorts projections when an activation dimension is nearly constant on Roleplaying but varies on a target. Dividing by the tiny source standard deviation inflates that dimension's target values, so it can dominate the projections. These are values the source-trained probes never saw at that scale.
rubric: Identifies dimensions with very small source variance but substantial target variance (or large source/target mean offsets)
Explains that scaling by source statistics inflates those target values, so they dominate or distort the PC projections

items.question: If Appendix D's Jaccard overlap were computed between the source-PCA probe ranking's top-k and the per-fold greedy subsets of Section 4.2, why could the overlap be low even if the source-discriminative hypothesis were correct?
items.answer: In Section 4.3, k and the reference set come from a greedy run on the full target dataset, and that run differs from the per-fold subsets in both membership and size. Jaccard overlap penalizes size mismatches and per-fold variation. Low overlap could therefore reflect a procedural mismatch rather than a failed hypothesis. The appropriate comparison is with the full-target greedy set.
rubric: Says the overlap can be low for procedural reasons and does not by itself refute the hypothesis
Explains that k is set by the full-target greedy run, whose subset differs in size and membership from the per-fold subsets

items.question: Appendix E says tactic-based directions are rated more general but are often called noisy, while the judge prompt says noisy directions should usually score 1 to 4. When could this combination make the interp rule miss the directions it is meant to keep?
items.answer: This can happen if the judge treats the noise flag on tactic directions as decisive and pushes their scores down into the 1–4 band. They would then no longer stand out above the lexical or stylistic directions. Because the rule keeps only the highest observed score, the selected set could then be filled by whatever happens to top the scale, rather than by general strategies.
rubric: Identifies the condition: the 'noisy' instruction lowers tactic directions' scores to the same band as surface-cue directions
Explains that because selection keeps only the highest observed score, the rule then loses its ability to prefer general-strategy directions

items.question: The greedy search starts from an empty set and stops when no PC improves target AUROC by more than 0.001. What does it return if the target signal is carried only by combinations of PCs that are each uninformative alone, and why does this matter for its role as a reference?
items.answer: No single PC improves AUROC at the first step, so the search stops with an empty or trivial subset. This makes the greedy reference understate how well a source-trained probe could transfer. It then fails as an upper bound on that target.
rubric: Says greedy returns an empty or near-empty subset (stops at the first step)
Explains that no individual PC passes the 0.001 improvement threshold, so jointly useful PCs are never added
Notes that the reference then understates achievable transfer (not a valid upper bound there)

items.question: Why would Insider Trading Confirm plausibly be easier than Insider Trading Report for a probe trained on Roleplaying?
items.answer: In Confirm, the deceptive act is an explicit false confirmation in reply to a direct question. That resembles the outright lies a model tells in Roleplaying. In Report, deception is an initial omission of the insider information, which is a different form of deception from the source.
rubric: States that Confirm's deception is an explicit false statement, closer in form to Roleplaying's lies
Contrasts this with Report's deception being an omission, a form less like the source

items.question: Based on Appendix E, why would the interp-selected subspace most likely consist of PCs described as communicative tactics, such as defensive hedging?
items.answer: The judge lowers scores for lexical-marker and stylistic directions and treats tactic directions as more plausibly general. Tactic directions therefore tend to get the top scores. The rule keeps only PCs that received the highest observed score in both runs, so those are the ones retained.
rubric: Says the selected PCs are likely the tactic-described ones
Explains that the judge scores lexical/stylistic directions lower and tactics higher, and that the rule keeps only the top-scored PCs

items.question: Why do both weight-based rankings in Section 4.3 use the same k, taken from the greedy run, instead of each choosing its own number of PCs?
items.answer: Fixing k at the greedy subset size means any difference from the greedy reference reflects which PCs a ranking picks, not how many it uses. This mirrors the logic of the size-matched top-k-by-variance control. It lets each hypothesis be tested on whether its ranking identifies the same kind of directions the greedy search finds.
rubric: Says matching k removes subset size as a confound
Explains that the comparison then isolates the identity of the chosen directions, relative to the greedy reference

items.question: Table 2 is dominated by low-index PCs, yet it includes PC27 and PC41. Why can such higher-index PCs rank highly under the standardized coefficient?
items.answer: The standardized coefficient is |coef| multiplied by the PC's standard deviation. A lower-variance PC can still rank highly if the source probe gives it a large enough absolute coefficient, which happens when that direction carries strong label signal in Roleplaying.
rubric: States that a large |coef| can compensate for a smaller PC standard deviation
Links this to the source probe relying on that direction because it carries label signal in Roleplaying

items.question: Why is the complement control in Section 4.5 built from the remaining PCs within the top 100, rather than from the full representation minus the selected directions?
items.answer: The selected set and its complement together partition the same 100-PC basis, with the rest of the pipeline held fixed. Any difference between them can then be attributed to the specific directions that were removed. Using the full representation would add directions outside the basis and confound the comparison.
rubric: Says it keeps the comparison within the same basis, so selected and complement partition the top 100
Explains that this attributes differences to the removed directions, whereas the full representation would add directions outside the basis

items.question: Why is the source-trained probe on all top-100 PCs needed to interpret a difference between the interp-selected probe and the full-representation baseline?
items.answer: The interp-selected probe differs from the baseline in two ways: it is projected onto the source PC basis, and it uses only judge-selected PCs. The 100-PC source probe isolates the effect of the projection alone. Comparing against it shows whether any gain comes from the judge's selection or merely from reducing to the PC basis.
rubric: Notes that the interp probe differs from the baseline in two steps: PC reduction and judge selection
Explains that the 100-PC probe isolates the reduction step, so the effect of the selection can be separated out

items.question: Would the interp-selected PC subset change if the logistic regression regularization were changed from lambda=10 to lambda=1?
items.answer: No. The subset is determined by the judge's scores on source examples for each PC, and no probe is trained during selection. Lambda only affects the probe trained afterwards on the selected subspace.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that selection depends only on judge scores of PC exemplars, not on any probe fit

items.question: Would the greedy-selected PC subsets change if the logistic regression regularization were changed from lambda=10 to lambda=1?
items.answer: Yes, they could change. Each candidate PC is scored by training a source probe with that regularization and measuring target AUROC. Changing lambda changes the fitted weights and AUROCs, which can alter which PC is added at each step and when the search stops.
rubric: Answers yes (could change)
Explains that greedy scores each candidate by fitting a regularized source probe, so lambda affects the AUROCs that drive selection and stopping

items.question: If the judge returned exactly the same scores every time it was run, would the two-run agreement filter change the selected subspace compared with using a single run?
items.answer: No. Both runs would assign the top score to the same PCs, so the intersection equals the single-run set. The filter only matters when scores vary between runs.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that identical runs make the intersection identical to one run's top-scored set

items.question: If the judge's scores varied substantially from run to run, would the two-run agreement filter change the selected subspace compared with using a single run?
items.answer: Yes. PCs that reached the top score in only one run would be dropped, so the selected set would shrink. This is the recall-for-precision trade the paper describes.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that PCs top-scored in only one run are removed, shrinking the set (trading recall for precision)

items.question: Would the ordering of PCs produced by the source-PCA probe ranking be the same for Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm and Sandbagging?
items.answer: Yes. The ranking comes from standardized coefficients of a probe trained only on Roleplaying, in a basis computed only from Roleplaying. No target enters it, so there is one ordering, as in Table 2.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that the ranking is computed from a source-only probe in the source basis, with no target input

items.question: Would the set of PCs used by the source-PCA probe ranking rule be the same for Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm and Sandbagging?
items.answer: Not necessarily. The ordering is fixed, but k is set separately for each target from that target's full-dataset greedy run. The sets are therefore prefixes of the same list, and they coincide only if the greedy sizes happen to match.
rubric: Answers not necessarily (they can differ)
Explains that k is set per target by the full-target greedy run, so different-length prefixes of the same ranking are used

items.question: If some non-ambiguous Roleplaying examples had their honest/deceptive labels flipped, would the interp-selected PC subset change?
items.answer: No. PCA is computed from the activations of the same examples without labels. The judge sees only exemplar text and activations, not labels. The basis, exemplars and scores therefore stay the same; only the probe later trained on the subspace would change.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that neither PCA nor the judge uses honest/deceptive labels, so basis, exemplars and scores are unchanged

items.question: If some non-ambiguous Roleplaying examples had their honest/deceptive labels flipped, would the source-PCA probe ranking change?
items.answer: Yes, it could. The ranking is built from the coefficients of a probe trained on Roleplaying labels. Changing the labels changes the fitted coefficients and therefore the standardized-coefficient ordering.
rubric: Answers yes (could change)
Explains that the ranking depends on coefficients fit to source labels

items.question: A team extends the basis from the top 100 to the top 200 source PCs and reruns the interp rule unchanged. Why might PCs that were selected before no longer be selected?
items.answer: The rule keeps PCs with the highest observed score, which is a relative threshold. If any of the new PCs earns a higher score than the previous maximum, the bar rises and the originally top-scored PCs drop out. The new PCs are also, per Appendix C, less aligned with SAE features, so they are less interpretable.
rubric: Says the selection can change because the threshold is the highest observed score, which is relative to the candidates
Explains that a new PC scoring above the old maximum would displace previously selected PCs

items.question: A team has plenty of labeled data from its deployment domain and wants the best possible probe there. Should it use the greedy procedure, and why?
items.answer: No; a target-trained probe is the better choice. The greedy probe still fits its weights on source data and only uses target labels to choose PCs, which limits it to source-fit directions. A probe trained on the target can place its weight wherever the target data suggests.
rubric: Recommends training on the target (e.g., the target-trained probe) rather than greedy
Explains that greedy keeps source-fit weights and uses target labels only for subset selection, which is a constraint a target-trained probe does not have

items.question: A team takes the greedy subset selected on Sandbagging and uses it, with a source-trained probe, on a fourth deception dataset never used in selection. Is the resulting AUROC on that fourth dataset an upper bound or a genuine OOD estimate, and why?
items.answer: It is a genuine OOD estimate for the fourth dataset. The upper-bound caveat arises because selection uses labels from the evaluation target. Here no labels from the fourth dataset were used: the subset came from Sandbagging and the weights from Roleplaying.
rubric: Says it is a legitimate (unbiased) OOD estimate for the fourth dataset, not an upper bound
Explains that neither subset selection nor weight fitting used the fourth dataset's labels

items.question: A team proposing a new source-only selection rule can afford evaluation on only one of the paper's three targets. Which should it choose, and what caveat should accompany its result?
items.answer: It should choose Sandbagging. It is the most OOD target and leaves the most headroom, which makes it the most demanding test, whereas Insider Trading Confirm is easy for the baseline and discriminates poorly between rules. The caveat is that the paper warns conclusions from a single distant target should be treated with caution.
rubric: Chooses Sandbagging (not Insider Trading Confirm)
Reason: most OOD and most headroom, while Confirm is easy for the baseline and discriminates poorly
Caveat: a single distant target gives limited, cautious evidence

items.question: A team deploys an interp-selected probe built mostly on PR-style or defensive-hedging directions to monitor a customer-service assistant whose honest replies routinely use cautious, diplomatic phrasing. What problem should it anticipate?
items.answer: The team should expect false positives on honest replies. Appendix E notes that tactic directions are noisy and risk false positives from legitimate uses of the same tactics. In this deployment, honest hedging is common, so the probe would fire on it.
rubric: Predicts false positives (honest replies flagged as deceptive)
Explains that tactic directions also fire on legitimate uses of hedging, as Appendix E flags

items.question: Suppose the full-target greedy run gives k=5 for some target. Using Table 2, which PCs would the source-PCA probe ranking select, and how many would it share with a size-5 top-k-by-variance control?
items.answer: The ranking would select PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12 and PC4. The variance control would be PC1 through PC5. They share only PC4.
rubric: Lists PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12, PC4 for the ranking (and PC1–PC5 for the control)
States that the overlap is one PC (PC4)

items.question: If the interp-selected probe beat all three of its controls on Insider Trading Confirm but not on Sandbagging, how much support would that give the claim that the judge captures general deception directions?
items.answer: It would give little support. Confirm is easy for the baseline and leaves little headroom, so it discriminates poorly between rules. Sandbagging is the demanding, more revealing test, and failing there suggests the selection did not capture something general.
rubric: Says it would be weak or little support
Explains that Confirm has little headroom while Sandbagging is the more revealing test of generality

items.question: If Table 2's top source-probe PCs had mostly been high-index ones (for example PC80 to PC100), which explanation in Appendix D would be undermined?
items.answer: Appendix D's explanation would be undermined. It says the source probe's top PCs are low-index because low-index PCs capture the most source variance and the probe is trained on the same distribution. High-index top PCs would contradict this variance-based account, meaning the probe's reliance is not driven by variance.
rubric: Identifies Appendix D's explanation that low-index dominance follows from those PCs capturing the most source variance
Explains that high-index top-weighted PCs would contradict this variance-based account

items.question: If the greedy reference on Sandbagging were barely above the full-representation baseline, what would follow for interpreting the interp rule's results on that target?
items.answer: The greedy probe indicates how much room any source-trained probe within the 100-PC basis has to improve. A small gap would mean little headroom on Sandbagging. The interp rule's comparisons there would then be uninformative, likely because the source basis covers the target poorly.
rubric: Says there is little headroom, so the interp comparisons on Sandbagging would be uninformative
Explains that greedy marks the attainable improvement for source-trained probes in the 100-PC basis (e.g., poor basis coverage of the target)

items.question: If the interp-selected PCs turned out to be exactly the top entries of Table 2 (PC7, PC8, PC11, ...), what would the interp rule fail to test that the paper motivates it to test?
items.answer: The paper motivates the interp rule by the possibility that transfer depends on a property not captured by discriminability on either domain. If the judge simply reproduced the source-probe ranking, the rule would amount to the source-discriminative hypothesis. It would add no test of any other property.
rubric: Says the interp rule would collapse into the source-discriminative (source-PCA ranking) hypothesis
Explains that it would then fail to probe a property beyond source or target discriminability, which is its stated motivation

items.question: If the greedy search were run on target activations re-standardized with each target's own statistics, while the source-only rules used source statistics, which comparison would break?
items.answer: The use of greedy as a reference for the source-only rules would break. The rules would be operating on differently transformed representations, so greedy's advantage could partly come from target distribution information leaked through the standardization rather than from the PCs it chose. The paper fixes standardization on the source precisely to keep all rules comparable in what they see.
rubric: Identifies the greedy-versus-source-only-rule comparison (greedy as reference) as broken
Explains that target statistics would leak distribution information and make the representations non-comparable

items.question: If the target-trained probe on the top-100 source PCs scored far above the greedy probe on Sandbagging, where would that place the bottleneck for transfer?
items.answer: The bottleneck would lie in how source-fit weights use the basis, not in basis coverage. A large gap would show that the 100-PC basis contains plenty of target-relevant signal. Yet even the best subset with source-fit weights cannot exploit it, because the weights are learned from Roleplaying.
rubric: Says the basis contains the signal, so coverage is not the bottleneck
Says the limit is source-fit weighting, since even optimal subset choice with source weights falls short

items.question: If Appendix E had shown the judge routinely describing narrow, specific patterns as broad sentiment or honesty directions, which design goal of the judge prompt would have failed, and what would that mean for the OOD scores?
items.answer: The goal of preventing overgeneralization, which the prompt targets by asking for the narrowest accurate description, would have failed. Narrow directions would then look general and could receive inflated OOD scores. The scores would no longer reliably separate general strategies from local patterns.
rubric: Identifies the anti-overgeneralization goal (narrowest accurate description)
Explains that inflated generality would make the OOD scores unreliable for selecting general directions

items.question: Does the paper show that mean-pooling over assistant tokens is the best way to aggregate activations for transferable deception probes? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Mean-pooling over the assistant response is a fixed condition of the setup, and no alternative aggregation is compared.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that mean-pooling is a fixed setup choice with no comparison to alternatives

items.question: Does the paper show that layer 15 is the best layer for its PC-subspace selection procedures? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Layer 15 is borrowed from Ying et al., where it had the highest cross-domain AUROC in their analysis. This paper evaluates no other layers, and it lists other readout locations as an open question.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that the layer was taken from prior work's cross-domain AUROC and no other layers are tested here

items.question: Does the paper show that its PC-subspace selections would also help nonlinear probes generalize? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The pipeline is fully linear, consisting of a PCA projection followed by logistic regression. The paper explicitly leaves extension to nonlinear probes as an open question.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that only linear probes are used and nonlinear extension is stated as open

items.question: Does the paper show that removing GPT-4o's ambiguous responses improves probe transfer? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Removing ambiguous responses is a preprocessing step applied throughout. No configuration that keeps them is evaluated, so its effect on transfer is never measured.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that removal is applied uniformly and there is no comparison with ambiguous responses kept

items.question: Does the paper present the target-PCA probe ranking as a selection method that can be deployed without labeled target data? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The ranking comes from a probe trained on target labels, and its k is set by a greedy run that uses target labels. It serves as a hypothesis test, and the paper reserves the deployable, target-free role for the interp rule.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Explains that the ranking relies on a target-trained probe (target labels), unlike the source-only interp rule

items.question: Does a low Jaccard overlap between two selection rules' PC sets (Appendix D) show that the two rules give probes with different target AUROC? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Appendix D presents Jaccard overlap as a measure of how far two rules draw on the same directions. Overlap describes set membership, not performance, and the paper does not show that low overlap implies different AUROC.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that Jaccard measures shared directions, not performance, and no link to AUROC is established

items.question: Why might the target-trained probe on the top-100 source PCs understate how much target-relevant signal the subspace holds for Insider Trading Confirm in particular?
items.answer: Insider Trading Confirm has only 122 usable examples once its 29 ambiguous responses are removed. With 5-fold CV, each training fold has about 98 examples, which is roughly as many examples as the probe has features (100 PCs). The fit is therefore unstable or overfit, so this reference may be an unreliable, likely low, estimate of the signal the subspace contains. Sandbagging, with 621 usable examples, does not have this problem.
